main_damage_causes: Collapse of the Diagon Alley and train compartment introduction scenes removes Malfoy's ideological grounding (blood-purity as inherited belief, father's political briefings) and his calculated social agency, reducing him from a complex antagonist to a simple bully

Omission of the wizard's duel trick removes the clearest demonstration of Malfoy's strategic cunning — his use of institutional authority as a weapon — which is the template for his antagonism throughout the saga

Consistent trimming of moments that show Malfoy's vulnerability when isolated (flying lesson confrontation) and his humiliation when his schemes backfire (caught snitching, called a liar) removes the dramatic irony and psychological complexity that make him more than a one-dimensional foil

Theatrical exclusion of the Borgin and Burkes scene removes the foundational character work establishing Draco's relationship with his father, his interest in Dark Arts, and his interaction with the Vanishing Cabinet — stripping complexity from both his present characterisation and his future arc

Absence of the post-suspension gloating sequence in Potions removes Draco's most politically active and viciously triumphant moment in the book, flattening him during the middle act into a background antagonist rather than an active schemer enjoying his family's power

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Hogwarts entrance hall, Malfoy's introduction before Sorting
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book the train compartment meeting (Scenes 21-27) is the formal introduction: Malfoy arrives with Crabbe and Goyle, notices Harry with 'a lot more interest than he'd shown back in Diagon Alley,' introduces himself with deliberate aristocratic flair, insults the Weasleys by name with specific knowledge ('My father told me all the Weasleys have red hair, freckles, and more children than they can afford'), then offers his hand to Harry as a calculated social gambit — a moment of genuine arrogance mixed with political manoeuvring. The Diagon Alley meeting (Scenes 1-19) also precedes this, establishing Malfoy's drawling boredom, class snobbery, and blood-purity beliefs before Harry even knows who he is.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film collapses both the Diagon Alley meeting and the train compartment scene entirely. Malfoy's first appearance is in the Hogwarts entrance hall moments before the Sorting, where he delivers a compressed version of the train speech ('Red hair, and a hand-me-down robe? You must be a Weasley') and the handshake refusal. The Diagon Alley encounter — with its drawling voice, boredom, blood-purity manifesto, and the detail that Harry was 'strongly reminded of Dudley' — is absent. The train scene, where Malfoy seeks Harry out specifically and makes a calculated social offer, is absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Diagon Alley scene establishes Malfoy before Harry knows anything about the wizarding world — his drawling boredom, his assumption of superiority, his blood-purity views delivered as casual common sense rather than villainy. This makes him a foil for Harry's open-minded wonder. The train scene adds the crucial layer that Malfoy actively seeks Harry out and offers an alliance — he is not merely a bully but a political actor who wants something. Collapsing both into a single hallway confrontation loses Malfoy's complexity and reduces the rivalry's foundation from a layered social and ideological clash to a simple snub-and-insult exchange.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Malfoy's dialogue in the entrance hall introduction
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 26: Malfoy's insult of Ron is richly specific — 'My father told me all the Weasleys have red hair, freckles, and more children than they can afford' — demonstrating that Lucius Malfoy has briefed his son on rival families, that Draco operates with inherited social intelligence, and that his contempt is ideologically grounded in old-family hierarchy, not mere personal dislike. The offer of friendship to Harry ('I can help you there') is a genuine power play.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 1: Malfoy says 'Red hair, and a hand-me-down robe? You must be a Weasley.' The specificity of 'freckles' and 'more children than they can afford' — and crucially any reference to his father's intelligence briefing — is removed. The line becomes a generic class-sneer rather than an expression of Malfoy family politics.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor but symptomatic: the trimmed line loses the detail that Draco's contempt is inherited, systematic, and father-sanctioned. This foreshadows the Lucius–Draco dynamic that becomes structurally important later in the saga. The damage here is small in isolation but part of a pattern of flattening Malfoy's ideological grounding.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 — Flying lesson, Neville's Remembrall
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 69-80: After Neville's fall, Malfoy bursts into laughter ('Did you see his face, the great lump?'), then seizes the Remembrall and taunts Harry by threatening to leave it up a tree. Harry demands it back quietly; Malfoy smiles 'nastily' and taunts him ('Come and get it, Potter!'). When Harry charges at him on his broom, 'Malfoy looked stunned' then 'trying to sneer, but looking worried.' When Harry calls out that there's 'No Crabbe and Goyle up here to save your neck,' 'the same thought seemed to have struck Malfoy' — and he throws the ball away and flees. This is a complete arc: Malfoy is brave when protected, exposed as a coward when isolated, and retreats. His reaction to Harry's aerial charge is genuine fear, not just competitive frustration.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 6: Malfoy grabs the Remembrall, taunts Harry ('What's the matter, Potter? Bit beyond your reach?'), flies up. Film Scene 7: Harry confronts him in the air. Malfoy says 'Is that so?' and 'Have it your way, then' before hurling the Remembrall. The moment where Malfoy is visibly stunned and worried by Harry's charge, and the specific beat where Harry names his isolation ('No Crabbe and Goyle up here'), which causes Malfoy to recognise his own vulnerability, is not present. Malfoy's retreat reads as a casual competitive choice rather than an exposed cowardice.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes early that Malfoy's bravado is contingent on his backup — he is genuinely brave-seeming in groups and genuinely frightened when alone. This is a core character trait that pays dividends across all seven books (most notably in HBP and DH). The film removes the explicit staging of this vulnerability, making Malfoy seem merely sporting rather than structurally dependent on protection. This is a meaningful early signal the film misses.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 10 — Forbidden Forest detention, Malfoy's behaviour with Neville
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 206: 'Malfoy, it seemed, had sneaked up behind Neville and grabbed him as a joke. Neville had panicked and sent up the sparks.' This is a specific, characterful act: Malfoy deliberately terrorises a vulnerable classmate for amusement during a genuinely frightening situation. It shows his cruelty is active and targeted, not merely reactive.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 10: The film does not include the moment where Malfoy sneaks up on Neville and grabs him. The regrouping after the false alarm happens, but Malfoy's specific act of deliberately frightening Neville is absent from the corpus evidence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A small but pointed character beat is lost. Malfoy's deliberate cruelty toward Neville — targeting the weakest, most frightened member of the group — is a consistent pattern in the book that builds his characterisation as someone who punches down. Its absence in the film is a minor flattening.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 10 — Forbidden Forest, Malfoy abandons Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 210: 'AAAAAAAAAARGH! Malfoy let out a terrible scream and bolted -- so did Fang.' Malfoy flees in pure terror, leaving Harry completely alone and defenceless in front of a figure that is effectively Voldemort. This is a deliberate, characterising cowardice: Malfoy abandons a classmate to mortal danger to save himself.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 10: Malfoy screams and runs with Fang, consistent with the book. This moment is faithfully rendered — the scream of fear and the flight are present. No damage here.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Faithful. No damage scored.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 10 — McGonagall catches the students, Malfoy's detention scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 174-176: McGonagall 'had Malfoy by the ear' and was shouting 'Detention! And twenty points from Slytherin!' Malfoy's response is to try to inform on Harry: 'You don't understand, Professor. Harry Potter's coming -- he's got a dragon!' He is dismissed as a liar ('What utter rubbish! How dare you tell such lies!'). This is a crucial beat: Malfoy told the truth and was disbelieved and punished. His informing on Harry — which was factually correct — backfired. Book Scene 186 confirms Harry had also forgotten Malfoy had gotten detention too, meaning they serve it together.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 10: McGonagall confronts the students in the corridor. Malfoy appears 'smugly beside her' and is given detention along with the others. The specific detail that McGonagall physically had Malfoy by the ear, had already caught him separately, and that he tried to report Harry truthfully but was dismissed as a liar, is compressed. The film renders Malfoy as simply smug at the others' detention, rather than someone who had already suffered his own humiliating comeuppance (caught while snitching, called a liar for telling the truth).
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version contains dramatic irony and character nuance: Malfoy genuinely tried to get Harry caught and was himself caught in the process, humiliated by being called a liar when telling the truth. The film's version shows him as simply smug and then deflated when he too receives detention. The loss of the 'caught while snitching, disbelieved' arc removes a layer of Malfoy's function as a figure whose schemes routinely misfire and who suffers his own petard-hoisting moments.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 11 — House Cup ceremony, Malfoy's reaction
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 219: 'Harry, still cheering, nudged Ron in the ribs and pointed at Malfoy, who couldn't have looked more stunned and horrified if he'd just had the Body-Bind Curse put on him.' This is a specific, savoured moment of Malfoy's complete psychological defeat — not mere disappointment but genuine horror and paralysis.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 11: 'Malfoy has a cringing look on his face' and later 'Malfoy angrily throws his [hat] on the table in defeat.' The anger and the cringe are present, but the specific 'stunned and horrified' quality — the Body-Bind comparison — is replaced by petulant anger (throwing the hat). Malfoy's reaction reads as sore-loser anger rather than genuine stunned horror.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor tonal shift: the book emphasises Malfoy's stunned incomprehension — he cannot process the reversal — while the film gives him an angry, petulant response. The book's version is more psychologically interesting (suggesting Malfoy is genuinely destabilised by failure, not merely annoyed). The film's version is a small flattening into generic bad-loser behaviour.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — Wizard's duel challenge absent
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 90-107: Malfoy challenges Harry to a midnight wizard's duel in the trophy room, then tips off Filch so Harry will be caught. Hermione correctly deduces 'Malfoy tricked you. He was never going to meet you.' This is a sustained sequence showing Malfoy as a strategist who uses social manipulation — a fake challenge — to try to get Harry expelled. It demonstrates his cunning, his willingness to weaponise institutional authority, and his political intelligence beyond mere bullying.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The wizard's duel challenge, the midnight expedition to the trophy room, and Malfoy's deliberate tip-off to Filch are entirely absent from the film corpus. The midnight corridor sequence in the film leads directly to the three-headed dog encounter through a different route (getting lost after the troll incident).
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the most substantial omission in the corpus. The wizard's duel sequence establishes Malfoy not merely as a bully who mocks and steals but as an active schemer who manipulates situations to destroy Harry through institutional means. His trick of issuing a fake duel challenge and tipping off Filch shows the same pattern he uses throughout the series — using adults and authority structures as weapons. Without this, Malfoy's antagonism in Year 1 reads as reactive and petulant rather than calculated and strategic. This is a meaningful loss of his agency and function as an antagonist.

damaging_scenes.scene: CoS Film - Borgin and Burkes (theatrical)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Draco is shown at Borgin and Burkes with his father. He examines the Hand of Glory with malicious interest, smirks at dark objects, and is humiliated by his father's cold rebuke about his grades. He also nearly discovers Harry hiding in the cabinet. This scene establishes Draco's home environment, his cruelty, his interest in Dark Arts objects, his complex subordination to Lucius, and critically his interaction with the Vanishing Cabinet — a detail with saga-level consequences in later books.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Borgin and Burkes scene is excluded from the theatrical cut per the non-theatrical exclusion note. The exchange between Lucius and Draco, Draco touching the Vanishing Cabinet, and his humiliation by his father are all absent from the theatrical film.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The theatrical film loses the scene that establishes Draco's genuine interest in and comfort with Dark Arts objects, the power dynamic with his father (which is central to his arc), and his interaction with the Vanishing Cabinet. The cabinet detail is structurally important to HBP. Without this scene, Draco reads as a one-dimensional bully rather than a boy shaped by a dangerous home environment. His father's cold dominance — 'I would have thought you'd be ashamed' — establishes the pressure and shame that drives Draco's arc across the saga.

damaging_scenes.scene: CoS Film - Flourish and Blotts confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Draco taunts Harry and Ginny, and when Hermione defends the Gryffindor team he calls her a 'filthy little Mudblood' unprompted and in the open, in front of a crowd including Mr. Weasley and Hagrid. The scene shows Draco's casual, public cruelty and his confidence in deploying the slur openly.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film retains the 'Mudblood' slur but places it at the Quidditch pitch confrontation rather than at Flourish and Blotts. In the film's Flourish and Blotts scene, Draco taunts Harry and makes the 'girlfriend' jab at Ginny, but does not use the slur there. Lucius immediately silences him ('Silence, Draco!') before taking over the scene entirely.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Lucius cutting Draco off mid-taunt reduces Draco's agency and makes him a subordinate prop in his father's scene rather than an active antagonist in his own right. The book Draco operates with swaggering confidence at Flourish and Blotts; the film Draco is shushed. This subtly diminishes his independence and makes his cruelty seem derivative of his father's rather than his own character trait.

damaging_scenes.scene: CoS Film - Quidditch pitch / 'Mudblood' scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, after Hermione's 'pure talent' remark, Malfoy calls her a 'filthy little Mudblood.' The reaction is immediate and collective outrage. Fred and George try to attack him, Flint has to hold them back, and Ron attempts a curse. Malfoy is shown as genuinely provocative and the target of near-physical retaliation from multiple people.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film reproduces the slur and Ron's backfiring curse accurately. However, Fred and George fly at Draco's throat and are held back by Oliver Wood rather than Flint. This is a minor structural shift but keeps the scene largely faithful in terms of Draco's characterisation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The core beat is preserved. The minor difference in who restrains Fred and George is negligible for Draco's characterisation. Damage is minimal here; the scene largely works as intended.

damaging_scenes.scene: CoS Film - Dueling Club (Serpensortia)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, after Malfoy casts Serpensortia, he is described as smirking and having conspired with Snape beforehand. Crucially, when Harry speaks to the snake in Parseltongue, the narration notes Malfoy looked 'stunned' — he did not anticipate this and it unsettles him. The scene reveals Draco's tactical cunning (using the snake deliberately to humiliate or harm Harry) but also shows him thrown by Harry's unexpected ability.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Malfoy casting Serpensortia and, when Harry speaks Parseltongue, Malfoy is described as looking 'shocked.' This is consistent with the book. The scene is largely faithful.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The scene is substantially faithful. Draco's tactical cruelty and his surprised reaction to Parseltongue are both preserved. Minimal damage.

damaging_scenes.scene: CoS Film - Polyjuice / Slytherin Common Room interrogation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, when Harry and Ron (as Crabbe and Goyle) interrogate Malfoy in the Slytherin common room, Draco reveals key information: he doesn't know who the Heir is, wishes he could help, his father told him to keep his head down, that the Ministry raided their manor and they have a secret chamber under the drawing-room floor with Dark Arts items. He also expresses specific relish that he hopes Hermione is the one killed. His petulance ('I wish I knew who it is') is an important revelation — he is not the Heir, and his ignorance humanises him slightly while his malice remains intact.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Slytherin common room scene preserves the core revelations: Draco doesn't know who the Heir is, his father told him the Chamber was opened fifty years ago and someone was expelled, and he says he hopes it's Granger who dies. The film cuts the detail about the secret chamber under the Malfoy manor floor and the Ministry raid detail, which were small but character-enriching moments showing how much Draco shares with Harry (as a trusted audience for his father's secrets).
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film loses the detail of Draco boasting about the Malfoy secret chamber and the Ministry raid, which in the book reveals that Draco is genuinely in his father's confidence on dangerous matters. This makes him more than just a school bully — he is aware of serious Dark Arts activity at home. Without this, the film Draco in this scene is slightly flatter, though the main revelations (not the Heir, hopes Hermione dies) are preserved.

damaging_scenes.scene: CoS Film - Draco strutting after Dumbledore's suspension
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book explicitly states Draco was 'strutting around the school as though he had just been appointed Head Boy' after his father secured Dumbledore's suspension. He gloats to Crabbe and Goyle in Potions that his father got rid of Dumbledore, suggests Snape apply for the headmaster's job (flattering Snape for political advantage), and says 'I expect you'd have Father's vote, sir.' He bets five Galleons the next victim dies and specifically says 'Pity it wasn't Granger.' This shows Draco at his most politically savvy and viciously triumphant.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This extended gloating sequence in Potions class is entirely absent from the film corpus. The film does not depict Draco's triumphant strutting period after Dumbledore's removal.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is one of the most revealing Draco sequences in CoS. It shows him leveraging his father's political power to elevate his own status at school, using flattery strategically with Snape, and revelling openly in Muggle-born suffering. The absence flattens Draco's characterisation during the middle act and removes the clearest demonstration that Draco understands and participates in his family's political maneuvering — not just parrots it. It also removes the specific beat that Ron nearly attacked him with bare hands, showing how viscerally threatening Draco's cruelty is.

damaging_scenes.scene: CoS Film - Diary / Valentine's corridor scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book, Malfoy picks up Riddle's diary after it falls in the Valentine's Day chaos, taunts Harry by pretending to read it, and Harry uses Expelliarmus to disarm him — the first time Harry uses Expelliarmus offensively against a peer. Malfoy then spitefully shouts at Ginny about her valentine as he leaves. This scene shows Draco's opportunistic cruelty and his ability to humiliate on multiple fronts simultaneously.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is absent from the film corpus. The diary is found by Harry in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom rather than being seized by Malfoy in a corridor confrontation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The loss of this scene removes a small but meaningful Draco beat: his opportunistic cruelty toward both Harry and Ginny simultaneously, and Harry's active use of Expelliarmus against him. It also removes Draco as the indirect catalyst for Harry discovering the diary's significance. The film's replacement (Myrtle's bathroom discovery) is functional but removes Draco's agency in the plot at this moment.

damaging_scenes.scene: CoS Film - End of year / Draco resentful and sulky
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book closes Draco's arc for CoS by noting: 'Draco was no longer strutting around the school as though he owned the place. On the contrary, he looked resentful and sulky' after his father was sacked as governor. This is a satisfying reversal that completes the arc of Draco's triumphalism and shows consequences for his family's actions.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's closing Great Hall scene does not show Draco at all. The Slytherin table is noted as not sharing the general celebration, but there is no specific beat showing Draco's deflation or his resentful reaction to his father's consequences.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The absence of Draco's closing beat — his sulky, resentful deflation — means his arc in CoS lacks a closing note. The film establishes his triumphalism after Dumbledore's suspension (in the book) and his father's scheming, but without showing the reversal, the audience doesn't see Draco brought low. This is a small but real arc loss.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (EXT. PADDOCK - HAGRID'S HUT): Malfoy skips the sneering commentary and goes straight to approaching Buckbeak
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 42-50 establish that Malfoy delivers a sustained, multi-beat campaign of sneering mockery at Hagrid before the Buckbeak incident: 'Oh, how silly we've all been! We should have stroked them! why didn't we guess!' and 'Oh, tremendously funny! Really witty, giving us books that try and rip our hands off!' — a calculated, contemptuous performance designed to undermine Hagrid's authority in front of the whole class.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, after Hagrid demonstrates stroking the book, Malfoy shakes his head and mutters to Crabbe and Goyle ('God, this place is going to the dogs...') but the extended sneering routine mocking the book lesson is omitted. The film moves quickly to the Buckbeak sequence, losing the full texture of Malfoy's deliberate, public humiliation campaign against Hagrid.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book establishes that Malfoy is a calculated social bully who performs cruelty for an audience, landing rhetorical blows with wit and timing. The film reduces this to a single muttered aside, losing the portrait of Malfoy as someone who weaponises public mockery. His cruelty feels more impulsive and less intelligent as a result.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (EXT. PADDOCK): Malfoy's approach to Buckbeak and insult
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 62: 'This is very easy,' Malfoy drawled, loud enough for Harry to hear him. 'I knew it must have been, if Potter could do it.... I bet you're not dangerous at all, are you?' — Malfoy's insult is framed as a competitive put-down of Harry first, then of Buckbeak, with his characteristic lazy drawl and social performance for the class.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 3: 'Give me a go at that thing. If Potter can do it, it must be easy. You're not dangerous at all, are you, you great ugly brute.' The line is largely preserved but Malfoy 'pushes past them roughly' and strides forward impulsively. The book's 'took over Buckbeak... patting his beak, looking disdainful' — the beat of Malfoy initially succeeding and performing confidence before the slash — is cut. The film moves immediately to the attack.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book shows Malfoy briefly succeeding (Buckbeak bowed to him, he was patting the beak) before his arrogance undoes him — a small but meaningful beat showing that his downfall is purely self-inflicted overconfidence, not simple stupidity. The film's version makes him look reckless rather than arrogantly miscalculating, slightly flattening the irony.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 4 (INT. GREAT HALL - NIGHT): Malfoy holds court with arm in sling
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 86-88: Malfoy swaggers into Potions 'acting as though he were the heroic survivor of some dreadful battle,' puts on 'a brave sort of grimace' for Pansy, then winks at Crabbe and Goyle when she looks away — a private, cynical acknowledgment that he is faking, showing his manipulativeness and self-awareness.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 4: Malfoy tells Pansy 'It comes and goes. Still... I consider myself lucky. According to Madam Pomfrey, another minute or two... and I could've lost the arm.' The theatrical self-pity is present, but the conspiratorial wink to Crabbe and Goyle — the key tell that Malfoy is consciously performing and knows it — is absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The wink is a small but characterful moment: it reveals Malfoy's self-aware cynicism and his confidence that he can manipulate others. Without it, his performance reads as straightforwardly theatrical rather than calculatedly cynical. It is a minor loss but reduces the layered quality of his villainy.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 (INT. LUPIN'S CLASSROOM - Boggart lesson): Malfoy mutters 'It's this class that's ridiculous'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 140-141: 'Only Draco Malfoy and his gang of Slytherins had anything bad to say about Professor Lupin. "Look at the state of his robes," Malfoy would say in a loud whisper as Professor Lupin passed. "He dresses like our old houseelf."' — Malfoy's mockery of Lupin is public, sustained, and aimed at humiliating him through class consciousness (poverty, shabby clothes), a recurring pattern across multiple scenes.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 5: Malfoy mutters softly 'It's this class that's ridiculous' — a brief, almost inaudible aside that targets the lesson rather than Lupin personally. The film contains no equivalent of the sustained, public, class-based mockery of Lupin's poverty that runs through the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Malfoy uses class snobbery as a weapon, publicly and repeatedly mocking Lupin's poverty to delegitimise him. This is a defining character trait — his contempt is rooted in social hierarchy, not just general antagonism. The film's version is a throwaway mutter that erases this dimension of his characterisation entirely, making his hostility to Lupin seem vague rather than ideologically grounded.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 6 (INT. LUPIN'S CLASSROOM - Snape substitute lesson): Malfoy passes caricature note
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 86-113 (Potions class) establish Malfoy's mode of antagonism in classroom settings: he uses Snape's favour to torment Harry and Ron directly and personally, leveraging institutional power. His taunts are verbal, targeted, and escalating — about Hagrid, about Black, about Harry's vulnerability.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 6: Malfoy draws a crude caricature of Harry being struck by lightning in his Quidditch robes and sends it as a paper moth. He also lets out a low howl when Hermione discusses werewolves. His antagonism here is more juvenile and impish — pranks and mockery — rather than the calculated personal cruelty of the book.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film substitutes bookish Malfoy's sharp, targeted verbal cruelty with slapstick prank behaviour (paper moth, howling). While not a major distortion, it edges him toward buffoonery and away from the cold, calculating antagonist the book establishes. The howl in particular makes him look silly rather than menacing.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 7 (EXT. SHRIEKING SHACK): Snowball ambush replaces Hogsmeade mud-throwing scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 193-216: Under the Invisibility Cloak, Harry deliberately stalks Malfoy, scoops mud, and pelts him — a planned act of retribution for Malfoy's taunting of Ron about his family and his gloating about Buckbeak's death sentence. Harry then engineers chaos (lobbing a stick at Crabbe, tripping him) with genuine comic wit, before Crabbe accidentally pulls off the cloak. The scene ends with real consequences: Malfoy reports to Snape, Snape interrogates Harry, and Lupin later discovers Harry had the Marauder's Map — plot-significant fallout.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 7: The scene is restructured as a snowball fight. Harry throws snowballs at Malfoy (still under the cloak), knocks Crabbe and Goyle down, pulls Malfoy's ski mask over his eyes and kicks him. The scene is played more broadly for comedy, Malfoy's taunts are directed at Ron and Hermione about their social class ('dream home... Weasel-Bee... don't your family all sleep in one room?') and he nearly calls Hermione a 'Mudblood' before being interrupted by the first snowball. Crucially, the scene ends with Harry revealed to his friends as a laugh, with no subsequent Snape interrogation scene in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, the Hogsmeade mud scene is a significant character beat: Harry acts with premeditated cunning, using the cloak offensively, and faces real consequences that advance the plot (Snape's interrogation, the Marauder's Map subplot). Malfoy functions as the trigger for Harry's recklessness and as a genuine informant whose report to Snape creates tension. The film converts this into a broad comic set-piece that dissipates into a snowball fight among friends, removing Malfoy's function as a plot-consequential antagonist and flattening Harry's morally complex use of the cloak for revenge.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 10 (EXT. near Hagrid's hut): Malfoy spying with binoculars, 'Father said I can keep the head'
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 232-243: After the hearing verdict, Malfoy walks back from Hagrid's cabin 'laughing derisively,' then stands inside the castle doors to overhear Hagrid's distress, before delivering 'Have you ever seen anything quite as pathetic? And he's supposed to be our teacher!' — a cold, public humiliation of a grieving man. This triggers Hermione's slap. The scene is about Malfoy performing cruelty as entertainment for an audience at a moment of maximum vulnerability.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 10: Malfoy spies on Hagrid with binoculars from a distance, gloating to Crabbe and Goyle: 'Did you see the big, fat blubbering oaf?! Oh, this is going to be rich. Did I tell you, Father said I can keep the head.' The film relocates the cruelty to a spying scene rather than a direct confrontation, and the line about keeping Buckbeak's head is a film invention not present in the book corpus. It makes Malfoy ghoulishly cruel but removes the element of publicly performed humiliation of Hagrid to his face.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene where Malfoy mocks Hagrid directly to his face — in earshot, as Hagrid grieves — is what makes Hermione's slap an emotionally earned explosion. The film's version distances Malfoy (binoculars, spying) and replaces the direct public mockery with voyeuristic gloating. This weakens the emotional logic of Hermione's reaction in the film, since Malfoy is not delivering his cruelty to Hagrid's face in the same way. The relationship between Malfoy's cruelty and the trio's protective fury over Hagrid is somewhat diluted.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 11 (EXT. SUNDIAL GARDEN): Hermione punches Malfoy; Malfoy calls her 'Mudblood' (interrupted)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scene 238-243: Hermione slaps Malfoy after he calls Hagrid 'pathetic' in the castle doorway. She then pulls out her wand and advances on him, forcing him to retreat into the dungeons. The confrontation is verbal and wand-based; Hermione's slap is impulsive, and she follows it with a wand-draw that genuinely frightens Malfoy. The specific trigger is his contempt for Hagrid as a teacher.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 11: Hermione jabs her wand under Malfoy's nose as he gloats about Buckbeak near the sundial. Ron tells her 'He's not worth it.' She then delivers a 'looping right to Malfoy's jaw, putting him flat on his back.' In film scene 7, Malfoy nearly calls Hermione a 'Mudblood' but is interrupted by a snowball. The punch is more physically dramatic than a slap, and the 'Mudblood' near-slur is displaced to the Hogsmeade scene.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The change from slap to full punch is a minor but meaningful tonal shift — in the book, the slap is an impulsive, emotional reaction; the film's punch plays more heroically. More significantly, the book's trigger (Malfoy mocking Hagrid as a teacher to his face) is displaced and partially replaced, slightly weakening the specificity of Hermione's protectiveness toward Hagrid as the emotional logic of the blow.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 14 (EXT. CASTLE ENTRANCE: Firebolt reveal): Malfoy's response to the Firebolt is reduced to slapping Crabbe and Goyle's hands down
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book scenes 180-185: Malfoy approaches for a closer look and delivers a pointed jab: 'Got plenty of special features, hasn't it? Shame it doesn't come with a parachute -- in case you get too near a dementor.' Harry fires back: 'Pity you can't attach an extra arm to yours, Malfoy. Then it could catch the Snitch for you.' Malfoy's pale eyes narrow, he stalks away, and goes to consult his team — a complete beat of verbal sparring that establishes the Quidditch rivalry as personal and witty.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film scene 14: When Harry reveals the Firebolt, Malfoy is present but his only action is to slap down Crabbe and Goyle's hands when they imitate testing the wind. There is no verbal exchange with Harry, no personal jab, no witty riposte from Harry. Malfoy is essentially a silent background presence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Firebolt confrontation in the book is one of the sharpest exchanges of the novel — it establishes the Harry-Malfoy rivalry as not just physical but verbal, with Harry holding his own and even besting Malfoy in the exchange. The film removes Malfoy's voice entirely from the scene, eliminating a key beat of the rivalry dynamic and Harry's confident wit in response. This is a relationship-level loss: the Quidditch rivalry between them, which is central to the third act, is stripped of its personal, adversarial texture.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Malfoy taunting Harry from a tree before the ferret incident
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: In the book (Scenes 137–138), Malfoy greets Harry on the ground with his 'familiar sneer firmly in place,' delivers a cold, calculated taunt about Harry not lasting ten minutes in the tournament, and positions himself as a composed, superior antagonist. His cruelty is deliberate and controlled.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Malfoy calls out from up a tree ('Why so tense, Potter? My father and I have a bet...'), which frames him as juvenile and physically removed. More critically, Harry responds by shoving Malfoy and calling him 'pathetic' and his father 'vile and cruel' — Harry escalates physically, making Malfoy's subsequent hex attempt feel reactive rather than the book's simultaneous duel. Harry dominates the exchange verbally and physically before Moody even arrives.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Malfoy is a ground-level, composed, intimidating presence. The tree perch makes him look silly and cartoonish. More damaging is that Harry's shove and insults reframe the encounter: instead of two antagonists at matched tension, Malfoy is made to look weak before Moody even acts. This diminishes Malfoy's menace and shifts the power dynamic away from the book's portrayal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — Ferret transformation and Malfoy's reaction
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 106–121 establish that after being transformed back, Malfoy mutters something with 'my father' audible, showing his instinct to invoke Lucius as protection. He is pale, watering-eyed with 'pain and humiliation,' resentful but cowed. Moody directly threatens him ('I know your father of old, boy'). Malfoy is genuinely humiliated but retains his sullen defiance.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: After being turned back, Malfoy simply runs away. The film reduces his response to physical flight. The crucial exchange — Malfoy invoking his father, Moody's counter-threat about knowing Lucius, Malfoy's resentful 'yes sir' — is entirely absent. The film also plays the ferret scene primarily for broad comedy (sending the ferret up a friend's trouser leg), and Malfoy's 'My father will hear about this!' is shouted before the transformation, not after.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The post-transformation exchange in the book reveals Malfoy's primary psychological weapon (invoking his father) and Moody's awareness of the Malfoy family's dark history. Its removal flattens Malfoy into pure slapstick victim. The 'My father will hear about this!' line is retained but repositioned as a pre-transformation bluster rather than a post-humiliation reflex, losing the layered dynamic of a shamed boy reaching for his father's authority.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 1 — Malfoy's introduction at the World Cup stadium
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 4–16 show Malfoy arriving with his parents, the Malfoys exchanging pointed social pleasantries with Fudge, Lucius making a cutting remark about Arthur Weasley's finances, and Draco giving Harry, Ron, and Hermione 'one contemptuous look' before settling between his parents. The scene establishes the Malfoy family's social status, blood-purity contempt, and Draco's mirroring of his father.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In Film Scene 1, Lucius appears briefly with Draco. Lucius delivers 'put it this way, if it rains you'll be the first to know' and 'Don't boast, Draco. There's no need with these people,' then 'Do enjoy yourself, won't you? While you can.' Draco says only 'Father and I are in the Minister's box, by personal invitation of Cornelius Fudge himself.' The extended social dynamic with Arthur Weasley, the contempt directed at Hermione, and Draco's individual characterisation in this scene are absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is Draco's key early-book moment of social positioning — showing he operates in his father's shadow, that he mirrors Lucius's contempt for Muggle-borns, and establishing the Malfoy-Weasley rivalry. The film gives Draco only one boastful line before Lucius shuts him down, which actually works against Draco's characterisation by making Lucius the dominant voice and reducing Draco to a child being corrected. The absence of Draco's individual contemptuous look at the trio removes a beat of his personal antagonism.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — No Malfoy forest encounter during Death Eater attack
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 19–38 show Malfoy standing alone, leaning against a tree, watching the chaos with 'pale eyes glittering.' He warns the group about Hermione being in danger from the Death Eaters in a way that is simultaneously threatening and revealing ('they're after Muggles'), calls her a 'Mudblood,' and when Harry asks if his parents are among the masked attackers, gives a chillingly evasive answer: 'Well... if they were, I wouldn't be likely to tell you, would I, Potter?' This scene shows Malfoy's complicity, his blood-purity ideology, and his first hint of dangerous family secrets.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This entire scene is absent from the film corpus. The Death Eater attack sequence (Film Scene 2) shows Harry, Ron, Hermione, and Arthur but contains no Malfoy forest encounter whatsoever.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the single most damaging absence in the corpus. The forest scene is where Draco transitions from school bully to something more sinister — a boy who may know his father is a Death Eater and who uses that knowledge as a weapon. His evasive answer to Harry's question about his parents is one of his most morally complex moments in the entire book. Its removal strips Malfoy of his darkest early characterisation, severs the foreshadowing of Lucius's Death Eater status at the graveyard, and removes the ideological dimension of his hatred for Hermione in a high-stakes context.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2 — Hogwarts Express; no dress robes mockery scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 56–70 show Malfoy seizing Ron's dress robe sleeve, holding it up for Crabbe and Goyle to mock, taunting Ron about money and glory, and then tantalising them about the Triwizard Tournament while making pointed remarks about Mr Weasley's Ministry standing. This scene shows Malfoy's class-based cruelty, his performative dominance, and his enjoyment of Ron's poverty specifically.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's train sequence (visible in Film Scene 4 context around the dress robes parcel) handles the dress robes entirely differently — Ron receives them by owl post at school, and no Malfoy mockery of the robes occurs on the train. There is no Malfoy compartment visit in the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The train scene is a key demonstration of Malfoy's specific brand of cruelty — targeting economic vulnerability, performing for an audience, enjoying Ron's humiliation publicly. Its absence means the film Malfoy never exploits Ron's poverty in this targeted, sustained way. The dress robes become only Ron's personal embarrassment rather than a weapon Malfoy wields.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 — No 'POTTER STINKS' badge distribution or Hermione hex scene
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 144–164 show Malfoy distributing POTTER STINKS badges, offering one to Hermione with the 'Mudblood' slur, provoking a wand duel with Harry, and then — after Snape's biased intervention — smugly pressing his badge. This sequence shows Malfoy's ideological cruelty toward Hermione, his willingness to provoke open conflict, and his exploitation of Snape's favoritism.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 3 shows the POTTER STINKS badges visually (students wearing them, the badge spinning from Cedric to Potter Stinks), and students hurling insults, but Malfoy's personal role in distributing them and the specific Hermione confrontation with the 'Mudblood' slur is not depicted in the corpus. The hex duel and Snape scene are absent from the film corpus provided.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, the badge campaign is Malfoy's sustained act of psychological warfare, and the duel scene shows him willing to hex Harry openly. More importantly, his targeting of Hermione with 'Mudblood' in this context — offering her a badge as an insult — is a key relationship beat showing his specific hatred for her. The film reduces the badges to background atmosphere without Malfoy's personal agency behind them, losing his role as active antagonist.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 5 — Second task; Malfoy slaps a boy but has no meaningful antagonist role
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book does not feature a notable Malfoy scene at the second task in the provided corpus, but the film introduces Malfoy slapping a boy and walking away with Goyle, which has no book equivalent in the corpus.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 5 shows Malfoy slapping a boy during the second task crowd scene, then walking away. This is a brief inserted moment of casual cruelty with no book basis in the corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: Minor issue. The slap is not based on corpus material and is a small invented beat. While it signals cruelty, it is generic physical aggression rather than the book's sharp verbal and ideological wit that defines Malfoy's antagonism. It slightly misrepresents the type of cruelty Malfoy typically deploys.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 2/end of year — No train compartment final confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 263–281 show Malfoy entering the compartment at the end of term, advancing slowly, noting that Harry has 'picked the losing side,' explicitly referencing their first meeting on the train and warning that Voldemort's return means Ron and Hermione 'will be the first to go.' He is then hexed unconscious by Harry, Ron, Hermione, Fred, and George together. This scene shows Malfoy's ideological declaration of allegiance to Voldemort's cause, his threat to Harry's friends, and his defeat by collective action.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene does not appear in the film corpus provided. The film's end-of-year content visible in the corpus (Scene 5, Scene 6) contains no equivalent compartment confrontation.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is Malfoy's single most ideologically explicit moment in Goblet of Fire. His declaration — 'You've picked the losing side, Potter... They'll be the first to go, now the Dark Lord's back' — marks the culmination of his year-long antagonism and his formal positioning as a figure who knows Voldemort has returned and welcomes it. Its absence removes the close of his arc for this book: from school bully to someone consciously aligned with the Dark Lord. The collective hexing also provides narrative satisfaction and closure to the year's antagonism.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film — No Hagrid half-giant revelation Malfoy gloating scenes
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 191–206 show Malfoy producing the Rita Skeeter article about Hagrid's giant heritage, gleefully noting 'he's just too ashamed to show his big, ugly face,' and then whispering 'missing your half-breed pal?' repeatedly to Harry while safe from retaliation near teachers. This extended campaign shows Malfoy using journalism as a weapon and his sustained, sadistic targeting of Harry's emotional vulnerabilities.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no Malfoy scenes around the Hagrid half-giant revelation. The Care of Magical Creatures lessons in the film do not include this antagonist thread.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This subplot reveals a calculated dimension of Malfoy's cruelty: he weaponises Rita Skeeter's journalism and exploits Harry's attachment to Hagrid specifically. It also shows Malfoy's cowardice — he taunts only when teachers are present to shield him from retaliation. Both traits (using media/information as weapons, calculating when it is safe to strike) are important to his characterisation and are entirely absent from the film.

damaging_scenes.scene: OotP – King's Cross platform, Malfoy taunts Harry about Azkaban
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Draco at the station is a background presence whose significance lies in what Harry fears he may have observed (Sirius as Padfoot), triggering Harry's anxiety about Sirius's safety. Draco's menace is indirect and laden with subtext about his father recognising Sirius.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Malfoy delivers a single taunting line ('I expect there's a cell in Azkaban with your name on it') and is immediately dismissed by Ron as 'only Malfoy'. The subtext about Sirius/Padfoot and the chain of consequences that drives Harry's worry about Lucius recognising Sirius is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book uses this platform moment to establish Draco as a conduit of real threat through his father – his presence here seeds the Sirius-in-danger plotline. The film reduces it to a throwaway jeer, stripping Draco of his function as a knowing agent of danger and flattening the scene to simple bullying.

damaging_scenes.scene: OotP – Umbridge's discovery of DA, Malfoy apprehends Harry in the corridor
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Malfoy uses a Trip Jinx to catch Harry in the corridor, delivers him to Umbridge, and is then sent by Umbridge to round up further DA members, acting as a capable, proactive lieutenant who savours his authority. He later has Harry's wand and taunts him in Umbridge's office, and is visibly greedy and eager when Hermione mentions Dumbledore's 'secret weapon', revealing ambition and cupidity beneath the cruelty.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus shows Malfoy bringing in one captured student ('Caught this one trying to help the Weasley girl') but the Trip Jinx, the active corridor hunt, and the extended office scene in which Malfoy handles Harry's wand and displays hungry greed at the mention of a weapon are all absent. The Inquisitorial Squad scene is explicitly excluded from scoring as cut material.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book this sequence is one of Draco's most consequential moments: he exercises real power, is trusted by Umbridge as an operative, and his greed foreshadows later Slytherin self-interest. The film reduces him to a functionary who delivers one prisoner, losing his agency, his menacing competence, and the complexity of a student who has effectively become a Ministry enforcer.

damaging_scenes.scene: OotP – Inquisitorial Squad corridor scene (cut from theatrical release)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Draco heads the Inquisitorial Squad, docks points from Gryffindor and Hufflepuff with relish, wields institutional authority over older students, and delivers the memorable 'New Head, new times' line. This is the fullest expression of Draco's ambition and his willingness to collaborate with oppressive authority for personal advantage – a defining character beat bridging his bully role and his later Death Eater trajectory.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene was cut from the theatrical release and is explicitly excluded from scoring per the non-theatrical material instruction. The characterisation it carries is therefore absent from the film.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The Inquisitorial Squad is the clearest book demonstration that Draco is not merely a playground bully but someone who actively seeks and exercises institutional power aligned with authoritarian forces. Its loss means the film never shows Draco as a willing collaborator with Umbridge's regime, which is essential groundwork for understanding his later complicity with Voldemort. Audience understanding of his arc is materially weakened.

damaging_scenes.scene: OotP – Department of Mysteries, Death Eater confrontation
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Lucius Malfoy leads the Death Eaters in the Department of Mysteries and is explicitly 'Draco's father' throughout – the scene makes Draco's family the face of Voldemort's operation. While Draco is not present, the book has just shown him as an Inquisitorial Squad member working in parallel with his father's Ministry machinations, creating a coherent father-son axis of antagonism. Draco's threat at the end of the book ('I'm going to make you pay for what you've done to my father') is directly informed by this moment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Lucius Malfoy does not appear in the film corpus Department of Mysteries sequence at all. The film corpus shows the DA arriving, finding the prophecy, and Sirius being tortured by Voldemort, but Lucius and the Death Eaters are not evidenced in the film corpus provided. Without Lucius's prominent role, the Draco-as-son-seeking-revenge beat that closes the book is robbed of its setup.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The father-son relationship between Lucius and Draco is a structural pillar of Draco's book characterisation: his cruelty is shown to be modelled on and enabled by his father. The absence of Lucius from the film's climactic sequence severs this link, making Draco's vendetta feel abstract rather than rooted in witnessed family humiliation.

damaging_scenes.scene: OotP – End-of-year confrontation, 'You're dead, Potter' / revenge threat
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Draco confronts Harry in the Entrance Hall with cold fury: 'You're going to pay for what you've done to my father.' This is a defining moment of Draco's emotional interiority – rare vulnerability beneath the malice, genuine filial love twisted into threat, and a forward projection of his arc into HBP. The scene shows him capable of real feeling, not just performative sneering.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This confrontation is entirely absent from the film corpus. The film ends the year without any Draco-Harry resolution scene following the Ministry events.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is the moment that transitions Draco from comic antagonist to genuine threat driven by personal stakes. It establishes that his hatred of Harry is now personal and familial rather than merely competitive, which is essential for understanding his willingness to undertake Voldemort's mission in HBP. Its absence collapses his trajectory and removes the emotional complexity that makes him a tragic rather than merely villainous figure.

damaging_scenes.scene: OotP – Hogwarts Express, ambush of Harry by Malfoy, Crabbe and Goyle
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Draco, Crabbe and Goyle attempt a premeditated ambush of Harry on the train home, only to be hexed into slug-like forms by DA members and hoisted into the luggage rack – a comeuppance that underlines both Draco's persistent vindictiveness and the DA's newfound collective efficacy. The scene also contains Ernie's pointed observation about Malfoy's mother, grounding Draco in family.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: This scene is absent from the film corpus entirely.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While not a major arc beat, the ambush scene demonstrates that even after the Ministry debacle Draco does not retreat – his malevolence is persistent and personal. Its absence slightly softens his closing characterisation and removes a satisfying demonstration of DA solidarity as a direct consequence of Harry's teaching.

damaging_scenes.scene: OotP – Quidditch match, post-match taunting leading to brawl
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Draco goads Harry and George into attacking him by making escalating comments about the Weasley family, culminating in remarks about Harry's dead mother ('remember what your mother's house stank like'). This scene is crucial: it shows Draco's cruelty has no floor, that he deliberately weaponises grief, and that Harry's response – though banned – is humanly comprehensible. It leads directly to Harry and Fred/George's Quidditch ban.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Quidditch match itself is not depicted in the film corpus. The post-match taunting and brawl are absent. The Quidditch ban, which is a significant plot consequence, is also absent from the film corpus.
damaging_scenes.explanation: This scene is one of the richest in the book for showing Draco's calculated cruelty versus Harry's emotional vulnerability. By targeting Harry's dead mother, Draco crosses a line that contextualises Harry's rage as grief, not mere aggression. Its absence removes a key moment of Draco's moral ugliness and eliminates the plot consequence of the Quidditch ban, flattening both characters.

damaging_scenes.scene: OotP – Care of Magical Creatures, Hagrid's absence / Thestrals lesson, Draco's sustained mockery
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Draco uses Hagrid's absence across multiple Care of Magical Creatures lessons to deliver cutting remarks about Hagrid's fate, leveraging his father's Ministry connections to intimidate. He also mocks Hermione's eagerness, imitates her, and gleefully aligns with Umbridge during her inspection of Hagrid – showing sustained, multi-layered antagonism that combines class snobbery, political awareness and personal cruelty.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film corpus contains no Care of Magical Creatures classroom scenes with Draco. Hagrid's absence is mentioned in dialogue but Draco's role in tormenting Harry over it, exploiting his father's influence, and collaborating with Umbridge during the inspection is entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: These scenes collectively establish Draco as politically shrewd, not just physically aggressive – he uses information about his father's influence as a weapon and positions himself as an insider in the Ministry-Hogwarts power struggle. Their absence reduces him to a background figure rather than an active antagonist whose menace is rooted in systemic power.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Borgin & Burkes / back courtyard (Film Scene 6)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book establishes Draco visiting Borgin & Burkes alone, secretly slipping away from his mother, speaking to Borgin in private, threatening him with Greyback, and asking him to keep an object safe and help him fix something. This is a solo, clandestine act of agency that Harry observes via Extendable Ears - the whole point being Draco is operating independently and covertly.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film replaces the solo Borgin & Burkes conversation entirely. Narcissa accompanies Draco into the shop openly. More damagingly, a back-courtyard ceremony is staged in which Draco, Narcissa, Bellatrix, and Greyback encircle a cauldron and Draco extends his arm to apparently receive the Dark Mark publicly and ceremonially in a group ritual. There is no private threatening of Borgin, no Extendable Ears eavesdropping, no evidence of independent scheming.
damaging_scenes.explanation: In the book, Draco's visit to Knockturn Alley is the first proof of his independent dangerous agency - he shakes off his mother, operates alone, intimidates an adult, and reveals strategic thinking (the paired cabinets plan in embryo). The film collapses this into a passive group initiation rite in which Draco is a recipient rather than an agent. The sinister intelligence and self-directed menace that make Harry's suspicions credible are lost. Draco becomes a ceremonially inducted follower rather than a calculating schemer.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Hogwarts Express compartment spying (Film Scenes 8-9)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Harry hides in the luggage rack under the Invisibility Cloak and overhears a substantial Malfoy monologue: Malfoy dismisses Slughorn's Slug Club snub with wounded pride, mocks Potter and the Weasley girl, speculates that when Voldemort takes over OWLs won't matter, and cryptically hints he may not return to Hogwarts because he has been given a mission - 'bigger and better things.' Crabbe, Goyle, Pansy, and Zabini are all present. The scene reveals Malfoy's wounded vanity, his ideological commitment, and his dangerous new sense of purpose.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film condenses Malfoy's train-carriage speech to a few throwaway lines about finding Hogwarts pathetic and not being around for Charms next year. The wounded pride over Slughorn, the sneer at 'the Chosen One,' the comment about Voldemort's new world order, and the meaningful exchange with Zabini are all absent. Critically, Harry does not actually hide in the luggage rack listening; instead he tosses a Peruvian Darkness Powder pellet through the carriage doors from the aisle - a prank framing that trivialises the sequence.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book scene is the primary vehicle for establishing Malfoy's ideological buy-in to Voldemort's cause, his wounded social status (Slughorn's rejection stings), and the tantalising hint of a secret mission. The film reduces it to vague bravado. Harry's listening-in, which in the book is a serious act of intelligence-gathering, is reframed as a prank. Audience understanding of why Harry becomes obsessively suspicious is significantly weakened.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Hogwarts Express compartment, Petrificus/nose-stamp (Film Scene 10)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Malfoy catches Harry, casts Petrificus Totalus, stamps on his face breaking his nose, says 'That's from my father,' drapes the cloak over him, treads on his fingers, and leaves him for the ride back to London. This is cold, deliberate, and personal - revenge for Lucius's imprisonment, not mere cruelty. The 'from my father' line is crucial: it anchors Draco's actions in filial loyalty and family shame.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Malfoy stamps on Harry's face and delivers the line 'Oh right, she was dead before you could wipe the drool off your chin' - a taunt about Lily Potter rather than a statement of revenge for Lucius. The 'That's from my father' line is absent. There is no finger-treading.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The removal of 'That's from my father' strips the act of its thematic significance. In the book it explicitly frames Draco as acting in service of his family's honour, connecting his violence to the Lucius-Azkaban throughline that drives his entire arc. The film substitutes a generic insult, making the act read as petty bullying rather than a statement of Malfoy's conflicted loyalty and motivation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Malfoy's Slug Club gate-crashing and Snape conversation (Film Scenes 23-24)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Malfoy is caught gate-crashing, looking visibly ill and grey-faced, with dark shadows under his eyes. Harry observes this closely and is struck by the absence of Malfoy's usual swagger. Harry then eavesdrops via keyhole on a lengthy, psychologically rich confrontation: Malfoy denies involvement in the Katie Bell attack, accuses Snape of trying to steal his glory, reveals he has learned Occlumency from Bellatrix to block Snape, refuses help repeatedly, shouts 'It's my job, he gave it to me and I'm doing it', and storms out in furious independence. The scene establishes Malfoy as genuinely dangerous, psychologically under enormous stress, and pathologically committed to proving himself.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The Slug Club gate-crash is present but brief. The corridor confrontation with Snape is drastically condensed: Malfoy says 'Maybe I did hex that Bell girl, maybe I didn't, what's it to you?' and 'I don't need protection. I was chosen for this. Out of all others. Me. And I won't fail him.' Snape says he swore to protect him. Malfoy says 'This is my moment!' and exits. The Occlumency detail, the 'stealing my glory' accusation, the revelation that Bellatrix is training him, and the extended psychological portrait of a boy cracking under pressure are entirely absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's corridor scene is the single most important window into Draco's psychological state at mid-arc. His Occlumency training under Bellatrix, his paranoid suspicion of Snape, his 'stealing my glory' outburst, and his refusal of help all characterise him as a boy under extreme pressure who is self-aware enough to be dangerous but too proud to accept a way out. The film reduces this to defiant posturing ('I was chosen!'), which flattens a complex internal conflict into a one-note bravado beat. The audience cannot understand why Malfoy is falling apart or what he has at stake.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Room of Requirement working scenes / bird experiment (Film Scenes 22, 29)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book never shows Draco inside the Room of Requirement during his repair work; his presence there is inferred by Harry via the Marauder's Map disappearances and Dobby's surveillance reports. The mystery and invisibility of Draco's work is a sustained source of dread. His internal experience of this labour is conveyed only obliquely - through his gaunt appearance, his skipping of Quidditch, his stress in Potions, his crying in the bathroom.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film grants the audience direct access to Draco working in the Room of Requirement on two occasions. In the first (Film Scene 22, set at Christmas), he places an apple in the cabinet, retrieves it with a bite taken out. In the second (Film Scene 29), he places a white bird in the cabinet, and when it returns it is dead. These scenes are presented as quiet, almost meditative character moments, with Draco handling the bird gently and looking 'lost.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: This is a complex case. The bird experiment scenes are not in the book corpus and constitute original film material. The gentle, mournful handling of the bird aestheticises Draco's villainy in a way the book withholds - the books keep his inner experience opaque precisely to preserve moral ambiguity and Harry's investigative tension. Showing Draco as poignant and tender-with-animals at this point reduces the dread of his unseen labour and slightly sentimentalises him prematurely, before the bathroom breakdown earns that sympathy. The mystery that drives a full half of the book's plot tension is partially deflated.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Astronomy Tower confrontation (Film Scene 38)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book's Tower scene is long and psychologically elaborate. Dumbledore keeps Malfoy talking, noting his feeble attempts ('so feeble I wonder whether your heart has been really in it'). Malfoy vehemently insists 'It has been in it!' He reveals the Vanishing Cabinet plan in detail, taunts Dumbledore about Rosmerta's Imperius, sneers about Snape ('he's a double-agent, you stupid old man'), draws courage from Dumbledore's praise, and admits 'I've got to do it or he'll kill me... he'll kill my whole family.' Dumbledore explicitly offers him sanctuary for himself, his mother, and eventually his father. Malfoy's wand hand drops a fraction before the Death Eaters burst in - he is on the verge of choosing differently.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film's Tower scene is substantially compressed. Malfoy reveals the Dark Mark, says 'I have to do it! I have to! I've got to kill you or he'll kill me' in a whisper. Dumbledore says 'Say that again, but aloud this time.' Draco slowly begins to lower his wand. The detailed confession about Rosmerta, the sneer at Snape as double-agent, Dumbledore's explicit offer of sanctuary for the whole Malfoy family, and Malfoy drawing confidence from Dumbledore's praise are cut. The scene is emotionally effective but loses the specificity of the book's revelation of Malfoy's plan and psychology.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film preserves the emotional core (Malfoy can't kill, his hand drops) but loses three significant elements: the detailed account of Rosmerta under Imperius (which explains the Katie Bell and poisoned mead plots cleanly), Malfoy's contemptuous dismissal of Snape as a double agent (which complicates his understanding of his situation), and Dumbledore's explicit offer of family protection (which makes Malfoy's near-surrender dramatically clearer and more poignant). The compression weakens the sense that Draco is genuinely choosing and that Dumbledore is genuinely reaching him.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Malfoy's deterioration arc across term (Film Scenes 13, 27, 32, 35-36)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book carefully charts Malfoy's physical and psychological deterioration across the year: he skips prefect duties on the train, misses Quidditch matches, is seen with dark shadows and grey skin, turns up ill at Slughorn's party, nearly cries when spotted by Harry during term, and is observed cutting himself during Potions and looking sulky and distracted. Harry tracks this obsessively via the Marauder's Map. Malfoy's periodic disappearances from the map are a sustained mystery. Dobby and Kreacher are deployed to tail him. The book gives extended interior access to Harry's growing obsession.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film references Malfoy looking 'different, almost ill' in one Hermione line (Film Scene 27), shows him disappearing off the Marauder's Map (Film Scenes 17, 28), and depicts him in the hospital wing briefly (Film Scene 35) and walking the corridor like a ghost (Film Scene 36). The Dobby/Kreacher surveillance subplot is entirely absent. The Quidditch match absence is not dramatised. The sustained, methodical portrait of a boy cracking under the weight of an impossible mission - weeks of failed attempts, physical toll, psychological isolation - is compressed to atmosphere and glimpses.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's most important contribution to Draco's arc is the slow, painful accumulation of evidence that he is failing and suffering - making the bathroom breakdown and the Tower scene emotionally earned rather than sudden. Without Dobby/Kreacher, without the Quidditch absence investigation, without the extended Marauder's Map obsession scenes, the film cannot show this deterioration with sufficient granularity. The bathroom crying scene (Film Scene 33) and the Tower scene (Film Scene 38) therefore feel somewhat abrupt: the audience is told Malfoy looks ill but has not been given enough accumulated detail to feel the full weight of his year-long ordeal.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Bathroom duel / Sectumsempra (Film Scene 33)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Malfoy is standing at the sink gripping it with both hands, his whole body shaking, actually crying - tears streaming down his face. Moaning Myrtle is coaxing him: 'Tell me what's wrong, I can help you.' Malfoy says 'No one can help me. I can't do it... it won't work... and unless I do it soon... he says he'll kill me.' This is a moment of complete private collapse, overheard accidentally by Harry, giving the reader direct access to Malfoy's despair and fear of death.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The film shows Malfoy crying at the mirror, the door easing open, Harry stopping - and then Malfoy wheels and immediately fires a hex. The emotional beat of private collapse is present but extremely brief. Moaning Myrtle's dialogue ('Don't... tell me what's wrong, I can help you') is absent as spoken lines. The specific verbal admission of 'I can't do it... he says he'll kill me' - Malfoy's most nakedly vulnerable moment in the entire book - is cut. The duel begins almost immediately.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The bathroom scene in the book is the emotional pivot of Malfoy's arc: the moment when the reader understands, with absolute clarity, that he is not a villain but a terrified child. The specific line 'unless I do it soon... he says he'll kill me' is the first time this is stated openly by Malfoy himself. Cutting this verbal admission in favour of a quicker transition to the duel means the audience never hears Malfoy articulate his own fear in plain terms before the Tower, reducing the cumulative impact of his near-surrender there.

damaging_scenes.scene: Half-Blood Prince - Snape corridor scene overheard by Harry at Slughorn's party (Film Scene 24 vs. Book Scenes 260-283)
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Harry presses his ear to a keyhole and hears an extended exchange. Malfoy accuses Snape of trying to steal his glory, reveals Bellatrix has been teaching him Occlumency specifically to block Snape, tells Snape to 'put me in detention' sarcastically, storms out furiously. The scene reveals Malfoy has been actively resisting Snape's help for months, is paranoid and strategic, and has genuinely internalised the mission as his own to protect.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Harry is in an alcove adjacent to the corridor and overhears only: Snape saying 'I swore to protect you, I made the Unbreakable Vow'; Malfoy saying 'I don't need protection. I was chosen for this. Out of all others. Me. And I won't fail him'; Snape saying 'You're afraid, Draco... let me assist you'; Malfoy saying 'No! I was chosen. This is my moment!' and exiting. The Occlumency detail, the accusation of glory-stealing, the months of avoided meetings, and the sardonic 'put me in detention' line are all absent.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The film version of Malfoy in this corridor scene is defiant but one-dimensionally so - 'I was chosen!' twice, with no further texture. The book's Malfoy is paranoid, tactical, sarcastic, and specific in his suspicions. His accusation that Snape wants to steal his glory reveals a particular kind of wounded vanity and strategic self-awareness. Without these details the character reads as a frightened boy who thinks he's special rather than a frightened boy who has thought carefully about everyone around him and trusts no one.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 (INT. MAIN ROOM - Malfoy Manor identification scene) - Bellatrix calls Draco forward to identify Harry
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 51: Draco approaches Harry reluctantly and with fear, keeping his distance from Greyback. His uncertainty ('I can't – I can't be sure') is driven by his own internal terror and reluctance — he is 'as scared of looking at Harry as Harry was of looking at him.' He walks away toward his mother of his own volition after his ambiguous answers. The dynamic is driven by Draco's private moral conflict.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Bellatrix physically nudges Draco forward ('Don't be shy, sweetheart. Get up nice and close'), making her the agent who forces him into proximity. Draco's hesitation reads more as passive uncertainty than as an active, internally-driven choice to protect Harry. The initiative and framing belong to Bellatrix rather than emerging from Draco's own conflicted conscience.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's version of this scene is one of the clearest signals of Draco's arc turning — his reluctance is a self-directed moral act. By having Bellatrix physically steer him into position, the film externalizes what should be an internal struggle, diminishing the sense that Draco is making a covert, dangerous choice and reducing his agency to passivity.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 8 (INT. MAIN ROOM) - Draco told to 'Call him' (summon Voldemort) and hesitates while Lucius acts instead
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: The book (Scene 94-95) has Bellatrix order Draco to pick up the wands, not to call Voldemort. The summoning of Voldemort is not assigned to Draco in the book; it is a separate, ambient threat. Draco's role in the escape sequence is to carry out Bellatrix's instructions mechanically.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Bellatrix orders Draco specifically to call Voldemort ('Call him, Draco'). Draco visibly hesitates, but then Lucius steps in and touches his Dark Mark instead, pre-empting Draco. This makes Draco's hesitation legible as a possible act of protection toward Harry, but it is immediately overshadowed and resolved by Lucius acting in his place.
damaging_scenes.explanation: While the hesitation hints at Draco's conflict, having Lucius immediately resolve it by summoning Voldemort himself removes any consequence from Draco's pause. A potentially meaningful beat collapses into a non-event for Draco, with his father absorbing the moral weight of the action.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (INT. ROOM OF REQUIREMENT) - Draco confronts Harry and demands his wand back
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 133-154: Draco confronts Harry backed by Crabbe and Goyle. He repeatedly tries to restrain Crabbe from killing ('No! If you wreck the room you might bury this diadem thing!'; 'STOP! The Dark Lord wants him alive –'; 'Don't kill him! DON'T KILL HIM!'). He shows strategic thinking, deducing that because Harry came for the diadem, it must be important. He is agitated, in command of his own reasoning, and morally distinct from Crabbe. He is wand-less after Crabbe's spell knocks his wand free.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: In the film, Draco is replaced by Blaise Zabini as one of the two companions (Goyle and Blaise rather than Crabbe and Goyle). Draco expresses a personal, almost intimate reason for wanting his wand back ('It doesn't understand me') and acknowledges Harry didn't betray him at the Manor. His commanding role restraining Crabbe from killing is entirely absent because the dynamic is different. Goyle starts the fire, not Crabbe, and Draco does not shout repeated warnings to stop killing Harry.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Room of Requirement scene is the last major demonstration of Draco's independent reasoning and his residual conscience — he repeatedly intervenes to keep Harry alive, showing he is not a killer. The film omits these interventions. The replacement of Crabbe with Goyle and Blaise also obscures the specific character dynamics, and Draco's strategic dominance over his companions is lost.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 19 (INT. ROOM OF REQUIREMENT) - Draco's wand is disarmed by Hermione rather than knocked free by Crabbe
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 153: Draco's wand is knocked out of his hand when Harry's Stunning Spell hits Crabbe, who lurches and knocks it free — it rolls out of sight. Draco becomes wand-less through incidental action. Harry then seizes the moment.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Hermione fires a spell at Draco directly and disarms him ('a BALL of SCARLET LIGHT bursts from her wand... and strikes his hand. As his wand flies free'). Goyle then steps in and fires back at Hermione.
damaging_scenes.explanation: A minor but meaningful difference: in the book Draco loses his wand through circumstance, not direct opposition. The book thus preserves the ambiguity of whether Draco would have acted against Harry. The film resolves the standoff more cleanly and aggressively, slightly flattening Draco's conflicted posture in the scene.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 21 (INT. CORRIDOR, post-Room of Requirement) - Draco lingers, looks back, begins to say something, then leaves
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 173-174: After escaping the Room of Requirement, Draco's only spoken line is 'C-Crabbe... C-Crabbe...' — he is visibly overcome with grief at Crabbe's death. This emotional response to losing his companion humanizes him at a key moment. He and Goyle are left slumped hopelessly on the corridor floor, wand-less.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Draco 'lingers briefly, then finally rises and follows, but as he reaches the end of the corridor, he looks back. He begins to say something, then continues on.'
