Ron says 'You're bloody well welcome! Prat.' There is no expression of grief for Goyle (who dies in the film in place of Crabbe). Draco silently departs after an ambiguous, unspoken gesture.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's moment of Draco mourning Crabbe is a genuine humanizing beat — the boy who has caused harm is confronted with loss and breaks down. The film replaces this with a wordless, ambiguous glance that is harder to read as grief. Ron's 'Prat' line closes the scene with an ironic note rather than pathos, further muting the emotional dimension of Draco's humanity.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 27 (EXT. COURTYARD - dawn) - Draco crosses to his parents' side in front of the assembled crowd
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 215-216: After the battle's climax, Lucius and Narcissa are seen 'running through the crowd, not even attempting to fight, screaming for their son' — the parents seek Draco. Draco's position and his reunion with his parents at the end of the battle is a brief, uncommented moment in a chaotic scene. There is no theatrical public crossing-over staged as a formal act of declaration.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Voldemort publicly invites people to declare themselves. Lucius calls Draco's name, Narcissa summons him quietly but absolutely. Draco — in front of the entire assembled school and Order — ducks his head and walks across the divide to the Death Eater side, 'avoiding the baleful glances directed his way.' Ron mutters 'He saved your life.' Narcissa hands Draco Harry's wand. Voldemort says 'Well done, Draco.'
damaging_scenes.explanation: This invented scene is the most structurally damaging moment in the film corpus for Draco's arc. In the book, Draco never publicly re-affiliates with Voldemort after his private acts of protection. The film stages a dramatic, public walk to the Death Eater side that — even if motivated by family loyalty — visually and narratively positions Draco as a traitor before the entire wizarding community, and has Voldemort praise him for it. This directly contradicts the arc of a boy who has been quietly refusing to commit to evil. It also transfers Harry's wand to Draco for no reason present in the books, creating a confusing and unearned wand-ownership implication. The scene undoes much of the subtle redemption work the character has accumulated.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 24 (INT. HEADMASTER'S OFFICE - Snape's memory / Dumbledore dialogue) - Dumbledore discusses the Malfoy boy's assignment
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scenes 190-199: The Dumbledore-Snape conversation establishes rich context for Draco's arc — Voldemort assigned the task as punishment for Lucius, it is 'slow torture' for the parents, Draco has a death sentence over him, Dumbledore explicitly says 'That boy's soul is not yet so damaged' and expresses concern for 'accidental victims of whatever schemes might occur to the boy.' Snape is instructed to offer Draco 'help and guidance.' Dumbledore distinguishes clearly between Draco being 'a frightened teenage boy' and a willing agent of evil.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: Film Scene 24 covers only: Voldemort's plan to have 'the Malfoy boy' murder Dumbledore; it is 'not expected that he will succeed'; if he fails, Snape must do it instead; and then the conversation moves directly to Harry being a Horcrux and Snape's Patronus. The film omits: Draco having a death sentence pronounced on him, Dumbledore's concern for Draco's soul, the instruction to offer Draco help, Draco blaming Snape for Lucius's fall, and the explicit framing of Draco as a victim of Voldemort's punishment scheme.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The book's Dumbledore-Snape exchange is the primary expository anchor for understanding Draco as a tragic figure — a boy weaponized by Voldemort against his own interests. Without Dumbledore's explicit statement that Draco's soul is not yet destroyed and that he deserves to be saved, the audience loses the interpretive framework that makes Draco's later hesitations and refusals meaningful rather than simply cowardly. This omission weakens the entire arc at its foundation.

damaging_scenes.scene: Film Scene 3 (INT. DRAWING ROOM - opening Death Eater meeting) - Draco described as nervously staring at the body above
damaging_scenes.book_baseline: Book Scene 17: Draco 'had been gazing up at the inert body overhead, glanced quickly at Voldemort and away again, terrified to make eye contact.' Book Scene 21: 'The hilarity mounted; Draco Malfoy looked in terror at his father, who was staring down into his own lap, then caught his mother's eye. She shook her head almost imperceptibly.' Book Scene 27: 'Draco shook his head jerkily. Now that the woman had woken, he seemed unable to look at her anymore.' Book Scene 32: 'Draco fell out of his onto the floor' when Charity was killed. These are a sustained sequence of specific reactions showing Draco's horror and dissociation throughout the meeting.
damaging_scenes.film_portrayal: The screenplay stage direction notes only that 'Draco Malfoy nervously stares at the body above.' The specific beats — his inability to look at Charity once she wakes, his jerk of the head when asked if he recognizes her, and physically falling from his chair at her death — are not present in the film corpus as scripted beats. The scene is compressed and Draco's sustained horrified reaction is reduced to a single atmospheric note.
damaging_scenes.explanation: The opening Death Eater meeting is the first opportunity to establish Draco's moral revulsion at what he has become party to. The book gives him a sustained, escalating sequence of horrified reactions culminating in him literally falling out of his chair. Compressing this to 'nervously stares' loses the gradation of his distress and the evidence that he is not a willing participant in murder.
